concerns: The headline results are selected by peak validation mIoU and reported on the validation set, with no held-out test evaluation despite a defined test split, so generalization is unestablished.

The three architectures are trained under materially different configurations, including different loss functions, batch sizes, and epoch budgets, undermining the claimed identical experimental settings.
The ViT segmentation decoding path is not described, leaving a core methodological component unspecified.

The three heterogeneous benchmark datasets are merged into an undifferentiated binary pool without dataset-level disaggregation, obscuring whether the comparison supports the stated industrial claims.
scholarly_quality.concise_summary: The manuscript presents an exploratory comparison but combines disparate benchmarks into an undifferentiated binary pool without dataset-level disaggregation. In addition, critical architectural specifics for the ViT segmentation head are absent, training regimes vary across compared models, and final reported metrics reflect peak validation checkpoint selection rather than held-out test evaluation, generating substantial scientific uncertainty.

Three different benchmark databases were used to ensure diversity in the studied materials, defect categories, 
and imaging conditions. 
• MVTec Anomaly Detection (AD) Benchmark [4]: Contains 5,354 high -resolution images categorized 
into 15 object and texture classes, including metals, fabrics, leather, and electronic components with 
defects such as scratches, dents, and cracks.  
• NEU Surface Defect Benchmark: A steel surface inspection dataset containing 1,800 images across 
multiple defect categories including crazing, inclusion, patches, pitted surfaces, rolled -in scale, and 
scratches.  
• DAGM 2007 Benchmark [16]: A texture defect benchmark consisting of 1,150 images covering six 
different defect categories.  
The merged dataset containing 8,304 images was split into training (70%), validation (20%), and testing (10%) 
datasets with balanced distribution across each split.

missing_information: No reproducible review or selection methodology was detected.

blocking_reasons: The headline results are selected by peak validation mIoU and reported on the validation set, with no held-out test evaluation despite a defined test split, so generalization is unestablished.

The three architectures are trained under materially different configurations, including different loss functions, batch sizes, and epoch budgets, undermining the claimed identical experimental settings.
The ViT segmentation decoding path is not described, leaving a core methodological component unspecified.

The three heterogeneous benchmark datasets are merged into an undifferentiated binary pool without dataset-level disaggregation, obscuring whether the comparison supports the stated industrial claims.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: The manuscript reports no held-out test evaluation or other evaluator-independent measurement; the defined test split is not used for the headline results.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Peak validation mIoU and Dice scores at the selected optimal epochs.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Training loss backpropagation and validation mIoU tracking used to select the best epoch checkpoint for each model.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: The paper claims that U-Net outperforms ViT and TransUNet with peak mIoU of 0.75, which matches the validation curve peaks reported in Table IV and the figures. However, merging completely disparate industrial datasets into an undifferentiated binary task obscures dataset-specific performance, and the claimed 'strong generalization' of ViT rests merely on validation mIoU matching training mIoU.
primary.evaluation_assessment: Evaluation reports peak validation mIoU and Dice scores across epochs. While a 10% test split is defined in Table II, the reported quantitative results appear to be selected solely by peak validation epoch rather than an isolated held-out test evaluation, leaving true test generalization uncertain.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: The headline findings report peak validation epoch metrics rather than an independently measured held-out test set evaluation.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Peak validation mIoU and Dice scores at selected optimal epochs.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Loss backpropagation (Dice Loss or Cross-Entropy) and validation set mIoU tracking used for epoch checkpoint selection.

primary.limitations: The authors acknowledge limitations including hardware intensity, the restriction to binary defect classification, and evaluation confined to controlled benchmark images without real-time latency measurements.
primary.method_assessment: The methodology pools three heterogeneous datasets into a single 8,304-image split for binary defect segmentation. However, crucial architectural adaptations are poorly detailed; notably, a standard classification ViT encoder is described without explaining how dense pixel-level segmentation maps are decoded back to full resolution, and training settings differ across architectures (different loss functions, batch sizes, and epoch budgets).
primary.quality_rationale: The manuscript presents an exploratory comparison but combines disparate benchmarks into an undifferentiated binary pool without dataset-level disaggregation. In addition, critical architectural specifics for the ViT segmentation head are absent, training regimes vary across compared models, and final reported metrics reflect peak validation checkpoint selection rather than held-out test evaluation, generating substantial scientific uncertainty.
